strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored question — the intersection of oversmoothing and optimization for GNNs — and its main message is novel and specific to GNNs: backward oversmoothing creates spurious near-stationary points once the last layer is trained, and this does not happen for MLPs (Prop. 2 gives an explicit counter-example), so the results are not a repackaging of generic deep-learning landscape results.

The main theoretical results are meaningful: Thm. 2 characterizes backward oversmoothing for non-linear activations (extending the linear-case 'gradient oversmoothing' of Park & Kim [25]), and Thm. 3/Cor. 2 prove that any δ-stationary output layer implies a global δ-stationary point with possibly high loss, with explicit rates involving depth L, spectral radius λ, and expansion rate α.

The proof strategy is instructive: the observation that, once the forward signal is oversmoothed, the backward recursion becomes approximately linear (since ρ′(H(k)) is nearly constant), allowing the oversmoothed backward limit to be exactly characterized by the average output error 1⊤B(L)/n, is a clever and reusable insight.

Assumptions are stated clearly and are verifiable (symmetric bi-stochastic P with spectral gap, 1-Lipschitz ρ, Lipschitz ρ′, bounded loss derivatives), and both MSE and cross-entropy losses are instantiated; the appendix contains full, reasonably careful proofs.

The paper is honest about scope: it explicitly states it does not propose methods to fix oversmoothing, that results apply only to vanilla GNNs without skip connections/normalization, and that only near-stationary (not exact minima) are proven.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is very thin: all experiments are on a single synthetic dataset (CSBM). There is no experiment on standard benchmarks (Cora, Citeseer, OGB), no verification that the theory's conditions (e.g., s ≤ λ^{-α} with the required small α, near-constant ρ′) actually hold during real training, and no direct test of the flat-region claim beyond Fig. 1.

Applicability to practice is limited: Assumption 4 (Lipschitz ρ′) excludes ReLU — the most common activation in GNNs — and the model uses symmetric bi-stochastic propagation matrices, full-batch gradients, and vanilla architectures. The restrictive expansion condition (α ≲ 0.21 for regression, ≈0.38 for classification, i.e., weights barely above contraction) further narrows when the theorem applies.

The result is about δ-stationary points and flat regions, not exact local minima or saddle points; the paper itself concedes it does not show the open set of bad parameters contains minima, and does not prove that gradient descent actually converges into these regions — the causal claim that this is 'the main reason deep GNNs are hard to train' remains an argument, not a proven statement.

Incrementality relative to [25] (Park & Kim, 2024), which already introduced backward/gradient oversmoothing: the contribution here is the non-linear extension plus the stationary-point consequence. This is real but the delta from prior work is moderate.

Reproducibility concerns: the code link is literally left incomplete ('the code is available at' with no URL), and experimental details (hyperparameters, architecture widths, how the MLP comparison is configured) are sparse. There are also typos and incomplete sentences (e.g., 'which will exists', 'log(1/δ))' in Thm. 3) that suggest the manuscript was not fully polished.

The reported exponential decay rates involve constants and conditions (ξq(α), β windows, n ≳ δ^{-2}λ^{-2αL}) whose practical interpretability is questionable; for real graphs like Cora where 1−λ ≈ 8.81·10^{-5}, the required depth L ≳ log(1/δ)/(ξ(α) log(1/λ)) is actually small, so how the asymptotic-in-L statement maps onto observed stuck-gradient behavior at moderate depth is not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored question at the intersection of GNN optimization and oversmoothing, which is well-motivated: oversmoothing theory typically assumes bounded weights, yet the weights could in principle learn to avoid oversmoothing, and the paper asks why this does not happen in practice.

The analysis is technically substantive: Theorem 2 extends backward (gradient) oversmoothing beyond the linear case treated in prior work [25], identifying the interaction between forward and backward smoothing at middle layers via the ρ'(H(k)) modulation term.

The main result (Theorem 3/4) that δ-stationarity of the output layer propagates to a global δ-stationary point, characterized through the norm of the average output error, is a clean and novel landscape statement, supported by a complete proof chain in the appendix.

The paper is honest about scope: it explicitly states it does not propose remedies, does not prove exact local minima/saddle points (only flat regions), and restricts to vanilla GNNs, with a clear outlook section.
The MLP counter-proposition (Prop. 2) is a useful sanity check establishing that the phenomenon is specific to GNNs rather than a generic deep-learning statement.
weaknesses: Restrictive assumptions materially limit practical relevance: P must be symmetric and bi-stochastic (excluding the standard random-walk matrix and, implicitly, typical normalized adjacency choices used in GCNs), ρ must be 1-Lipschitz with |ρ(x)|≤|x| and Lipschitz derivative (explicitly excluding ReLU, the workhorse activation), and only vanilla GNNs without skip connections or normalization are covered. The authors acknowledge this, but it leaves the 'why GNNs are hard to train' claim applying to a narrow architecture class.

The quantitative conditions in Theorem 3/Corollary 2 appear practically vacuous: the depth requirement L ≳ log(1/δ)/(ξ(α)log(1/λ)) with log(1/λ) ≈ 10^-4 for Cora/Citeseer (as computed on p.3) implies depths on the order of 10^4–10^5, and the sample requirement n ≳ δ^{-2}λ^{-2αL} grows exponentially in L. No discussion of whether the constants are achievable in realistic regimes is provided, so the asymptotic results may have little bearing on the empirically observed stalling at moderate depths (k=40 in Fig. 1).

Empirical support is thin: all experiments use a single CSBM synthetic dataset; no real graph benchmarks (Cora, Citeseer, OGB) are used beyond quoting spectral gaps. The central practical narrative (last layer trains first, whole network stalls) rests on one figure with one seed count and no ablations over depth, activation, or propagation matrix.

Novelty over the closest prior work [25] is incremental for the backward-oversmoothing component itself (extension from linear to nonlinear ρ); the genuinely new part is the stationary-point consequence, whose practical force is undercut by the points above and by the fact that only 'near'-stationary flat regions are shown, not minima or saddles that first-order methods provably cannot escape.

Reproducibility and presentation issues: the code link is dangling ('the code is available at' with no URL); there are multiple typos and minor errors (e.g., 'the whole GNN is at a stationary point' overclaiming exact stationarity vs. δ-stationarity in the abstract, broken reference [23] URL, truncated [26], missing norm subscript in Eq. (15), stray parenthesis in Theorem 3). Fig. 1 lacks error bars and experimental details.

The 'spurious stationary point' framing in the abstract and title overstates what is proven: what is established is the existence of open flat regions of high loss, not stationary points in the classical sense, and the escape-difficulty argument ('informally, it will be difficult...') is not formalized.

strengths: Original and interesting angle: the paper examines oversmoothing through the lens of optimization, a relatively under-explored intersection, and introduces the notion of backward oversmoothing for general (non-linear) activations, going beyond the linear-case analysis of Park & Kim [25].

The main results are meaningful: Thm. 3 shows that a trained last layer forces the whole deep GNN into a near-stationary point, and Cor. 2 shows such points can have high loss; Prop. 2 provides an MLP counterexample showing the phenomenon is specific to GNNs, which strengthens the claim of novelty.

The key technical insight (the backward recursion becomes approximately linear when the forward signal is oversmoothed, allowing an explicit characterization of the oversmoothed limit in terms of the average output error, Thm. 4) is clean and clearly explained in the sketch of proof.

Complete proofs are provided in the appendix, along with supporting experiments (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2) on GNN vs MLP gradient norms and forward/backward pairwise differences, and code is said to be released.

Honest treatment of limitations: the authors explicitly state that results apply only to vanilla GNNs, that no new mitigation method is proposed, and that they show a 'bad flat region' rather than exact local minima or saddles.
weaknesses: Limited scope of applicability: results hold only for vanilla GNNs without skip connections, normalization, or other standard anti-oversmoothing mechanisms, and for symmetric bi-stochastic propagation matrices (excluding, e.g., the common non-symmetric random-walk normalization). This significantly reduces practical relevance.

Assumption 4 (ρ' Lipschitz, differentiable ρ) excludes ReLU, arguably the most common activation; only smooth surrogates like softplus are covered, which weakens empirical transferability of the theory.

The empirical evidence is thin: experiments use only synthetic CSBM data; no real-graph experiments (e.g., Cora/Citeseer training dynamics beyond the λ values quoted) are shown to support the claim that spurious stationary points are 'the main reason why deep GNNs are hard to train'. This causal claim is somewhat overclaimed relative to the evidence, which only establishes existence of bad flat regions.

The 'spurious stationary points' are δ-near-stationary points, and the constructed example (Cor. 2) sets W(L) = 0; the paper itself concedes it does not show exact local minima or saddle points. The relationship between the theory and actual training stagnation (Fig. 1) remains suggestive rather than established.

The quantitative conditions are restrictive: the expansion rate must satisfy α ≲ 0.21 (regression) or ≲ 0.38 (classification), L and n must grow with log(1/δ), and the required output-layer stationarity δ̄ scales like λ^{αL}, which is extremely small for large L; the practical reach of Thm. 3 under realistic training settings is not thoroughly discussed.

Presentation issues: the code URL is missing ('the code is available at' with no link), references [22] and [23] are near-duplicates, [26] has a broken URL, and there are several typos (e.g., 'will exists', mismatched parentheses in Thm 3).

No analysis of whether standard fixes (residual connections, normalization) remove or merely soften the phenomenon, which limits the actionable value of the results at present (acknowledged as future work).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored question — the interaction between oversmoothing and optimization in GNNs — and its core insight (backward oversmoothing producing spurious near-stationary points) is novel. The main results (Thm 2, Thm 3/4, Cor 2) hold for non-linear activations and non-symmetric stochastic propagation matrices, going beyond Park & Kim [26], which the authors convincingly argue is limited to the linear case and contains an error regarding symmetric P.

The analysis is technically careful: full proofs with explicit constants are provided, including a refined symmetric-P case, a useful technical toolbox (Lemmas 1–4), and a clean decomposition of the backward signal (Eq. 25). The observation that the backward recursion becomes 'almost linear' once the forward signal is oversmoothed — enabling an explicit characterization of the oversmoothed backward limit even with non-linear ρ — is an elegant and insightful mechanism.

The paper is honest about its limitations: it explicitly flags that forward oversmoothing in the 'non-linear ρ, non-symmetric P' regime is an open problem (so results are conditional on Definition 1), acknowledges that the DF assumption is a 'proof artifact', and clearly scopes the work to vanilla GNNs without proposing mitigation methods.

The GNN-vs-MLP contrast (Prop 2) is a valuable sanity check establishing that the phenomenon is specific to graph architectures, and Prop 1 nicely separates backward oversmoothing from vanishing gradients.

Empirical illustrations across several real (Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, WikiCS) and synthetic datasets qualitatively corroborate the theory, including the prediction of middle-layer backward oversmoothing and the dependence on λ.
weaknesses: The central theorems are conditional on forward oversmoothing (Def. 1) holding, yet the paper itself shows condition (11) fails on most real datasets (Table 1: ||J⊥PJ⊥||₂ > 1 on 5 of 6 datasets) and cannot prove forward oversmoothing in the targeted non-linear, non-symmetric regime. The theory is thus validated empirically rather than rigorously on the very settings the experiments study, weakening the tightness between theory and evidence.

The quantitative relevance of Theorem 3 for practical settings is unclear: the required depth L ≳ log(1/(DFδ))/(ξq(α)log(1/λ)) involves ξq(α) ≈ 0.2–0.4 and, with real-data values of λ ≈ 0.9–0.98 (Table 1), plausibly demands depths of thousands of layers for meaningful δ; constants like s^L and A_L in the bounds may be very large. The paper does not discuss whether the theorem's regime is actually attained at L = 100 in the experiments.

The causal story 'last layer gets trained → whole GNN becomes stationary → high-loss flat regions' is only an implication (IF the last layer is δWL-stationary THEN global δ-stationarity). The claim that this explains why deep GNNs are hard to train rests on the informal premise that the last layer is 'exceedingly easy to train', which is asserted but never formally proven, and the experiments only loosely support it via gradient-norm decay curves.

Corollary 2 constructs a high-loss flat region essentially around W_L = 0 with centered labels — a somewhat special construction. The abstract's claim of 'many spurious stationary points' is stronger than what is exhibited (one family of flat regions, with the authors conceding others are 'likely').

The experimental section is illustrative rather than a convincing evaluation: only 100-layer vanilla GNNs, classification datasets converted to regression with MSE (explicitly because it 'exacerbates' the phenomenon), all nodes treated as labeled, and a hand-picked initialization Id + εN. No code or reproducibility artifacts are mentioned.

Proposition 1 relies on a trivial constant-signal GNN (ρ = Id, W = 1, constant input and zero labels), which limits its interest as evidence that backward oversmoothing is distinct from vanishing gradients in any meaningful setting.

Presentation issues: several typos and grammar slips ('wityh', 'A crucial ingredients', 'does not necessarily holds', 'these methods ... future work will have to theoretically analyze'), duplicated references [23]/[24] with a malformed URL, and Fig. 1's mixed-placement figure caption. While minor, they suggest the manuscript was not fully polished.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored question — why deep GNNs fail to train despite theoretically being able to avoid oversmoothing — and the optimization-landscape perspective is a genuinely interesting angle distinct from the usual expressivity/oversmoothing analyses.

The main mechanism (interaction between forward smoothing and the ρ'(H^(k)) modulation in the backward recursion, which makes the backward recursion effectively linear and thus characterizable) is an insightful observation that enables results for non-linear activations and non-symmetric stochastic P, beyond the linear/symmetric settings of prior work (e.g., Park & Kim [26]).

The proofs (Thms. 1–5, Cor. 1–2, Props. 1–2) are reasonably self-contained and technically careful; the paper correctly identifies and explains a flaw in the proof of Park & Kim [26] regarding non-symmetric P, which is a useful clarification for the community.
The separation result against MLPs (Prop. 2) is a nice touch, showing the spurious-stationary-point phenomenon is specific to GNNs rather than a generic deep learning artifact.

The paper is honest about its scope: it clearly states that it analyzes only vanilla GNNs, defers mitigation strategies to future work, and openly acknowledges that forward oversmoothing for the non-symmetric, non-linear case remains unproven.
weaknesses: The central results rest on an unproven assumption: forward oversmoothing (Def. 1) is taken as a hypothesis, yet the paper itself emphasizes that forward oversmoothing is not established for the 'non-linear ρ, non-symmetric P' case — which is precisely the general setting the paper claims to handle. Notably, Table 1 shows ‖J⊥PJ⊥‖₂ > 1 (violating condition (11) of Thm. 1) on 4 of 6 experimental datasets, so the theory's own conditions are not satisfied on most of the empirical testbeds, leaving a substantial theory–practice gap.

The main theorem (Thm. 3) is conditional on W^(L) being at a δ-stationary point, but the paper provides no theory for when or why the last layer reaches stationarity quickly; this pivotal step is only supported by informal observations from small illustrative experiments. The practical claim that 'as soon as the last layer is trained, the whole GNN is stuck' is therefore only loosely connected to the formal result.

The significance of the spurious-stationary-point result is limited: Cor. 2 constructs a flat high-loss region essentially around W_L = 0 with centered labels and small last-layer weights, which is a somewhat contrived scenario; whether the identified stationary regions are what gradient descent actually visits in realistic settings is not established.

The assumption s ⩽ λ^{-α} with small α (≈0.21 for regression) forces the weights to be nearly contracting throughout — close to the regime where oversmoothing is inevitable by design. This weakens the punchline that 'GNNs could learn not to oversmooth but don't', since the theory largely restricts itself to the regime where they cannot.

The empirical validation is thin: only 6 small datasets, full-batch training, all classification tasks converted to regression (with labels cast to integers), a special initialization (Id + εN) chosen specifically so the theorems' assumptions hold, and no comparison against existing optimization diagnoses. The experiments are illustrative rather than evidentiary for the paper's practical claims.

Several claims about relevance to practice are asserted rather than shown: no connection to modern GNN architectures (skip connections, normalization are only discussed informally), no demonstration that the identified flat regions cause the observed training failures at scale, and no predictive quantitative check of the exponential rates beyond rough estimates of λ_f.

Presentation issues: a duplicated reference ([23] and [24] are the same paper with a malformed URL), typos ('wityh', 'Theorem 2 describe', 'A crucial ingredients'), and dense notation (multiple constants C1–C3, AL, εn, ξq(α)) make the results harder to parse than necessary.

Reproducibility is questionable: no code is mentioned, and the experimental protocol involves several ad hoc choices (ε magnitude, weight initialization, label casting) that would be needed to reproduce Fig. 2–3.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored question: the intersection of optimization theory and oversmoothing in GNNs. Framing 'backward oversmoothing' as the mechanism behind spurious stationary points is an interesting and novel angle, distinct from the common approach of adapting MLP results to GNNs.

The main theoretical contribution is non-trivial: Theorem 2 handles the non-linear activation case (via the interplay of ρ'(H(k)) modulation with forward oversmoothing) and non-symmetric stochastic propagation matrices, which prior work (notably Park & Kim [26]) did not address. The observation that the backward signal becomes effectively linear once the forward signal is oversmoothed, allowing the limit to be characterized via (P^T)^k → π1_n^T, is a clean and clever insight.

The main result (Thm. 3/4) linking δ-stationarity of the last layer to global δ-stationarity, with the δ depending on the average output error ε_n, is a meaningful structural statement about the GNN loss landscape. Corollary 2's construction of flat, high-loss regions is an unusual and interesting landscape result.

Proposition 2 (the MLP counter-example) is valuable: it demonstrates the results are specific to GNNs rather than a generic property of deep networks, strengthening the significance of the contribution.

The paper is clearly written, with informative proof sketches, careful assumptions stated upfront, and honest discussion of limitations: it explicitly acknowledges that the 'non-linear ρ, non-symmetric P' forward oversmoothing case remains open, that no mitigation methods are proposed, and that mitigation strategies are deferred to future work. The appendix proofs are complete and largely verifiable.

The related work section is thorough and includes a specific, checkable critique of the error in Park & Kim [26] regarding symmetric vs. stochastic matrices, which contextualizes the contribution well.
weaknesses: The empirical support is thin and somewhat artificial. The experiments (App. B) are illustrative rather than convincing: they use full-batch training, no train/test splits, convert classification tasks to regression with integer labels (justified by the MSE loss exacerbating the phenomenon), and initialize weights as Id + εN to force s ≈ 1. These choices tailor the setting toward the theory's regime, so the experiments confirm the theorems but provide limited evidence that the phenomenon affects standard GNN training in practice.

The practical reach of the main results is limited by the regime they require. Theorems 3/4 need s ≤ λ^(-α) with α below ~0.38 (q=1) or ~0.21 (q=2) and L large; since λ is often close to 1 (e.g., 0.97-0.99 for Cora/Citeseer/Pubmed per Table 1), the required depths and the tightness of the bounds in realistic settings are unclear. The paper itself notes the effect is 'less clear' on three of the six datasets.

Key claims rest on unproven assumptions: forward oversmoothing is assumed (Def. 1) because condition (11) fails for real datasets (Table 1 shows ||J^⊥PJ^⊥|| > 1 for Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, WikiCS). The authors are honest about this gap, but it means the main theorems are conditional on a hypothesis that is not established for the very datasets used in the experiments.

Corollary 2 (spurious stationary points with high loss) requires restrictive extra conditions: centered labels, W_L small (||W_L|| ≤ ε_WL), and a specific depth condition. The constructed region may not be representative of what optimizers encounter; the claim that 'many other flat regions... could be constructed' is asserted without proof or evidence.

The theory covers only vanilla GNNs with a single fixed propagation matrix P and no skip connections, normalization, or attention. Given that essentially all practical GNNs use these components, the applicability of the results to modern architectures is deferred entirely to future work, reducing immediate significance for practitioners.
Reproducibility is not addressed: no mention of code release or seeds/hyperparameters (beyond initialization scheme) for the experiments in App. B.

Some presentation issues: Figure 1 caption contains a typo ('wityh'), and the overall flow would benefit from an explicit table of assumptions and where they are used, given the number of assumptions (1-5 plus Def. 1).
